name: pay-first-won
about: One concept clearly did well over many leads and one spent for nothing.

area.label: Fixture Yard, IL
area.reason: Fixture: drivers within a day's drive of the yard.

subject_matter.in_our_words: A small fleet where dispatch knows your name

history.text: Boostpoint 2026 benchmark, CDL drivers on Meta: an ad costing more than $42.00 per lead after 5 leads, or $85.00 spent with no lead, is where pausing is suggested.
Our ads with hook pay_first (pay first) and scene equipment_on_road (truck on the road) spent $612.40 in the last 28 days over 48210 impressions and brought 31 leads, $19.75 per lead.
Our ads with hook life_first (life first) and scene home_street (home street) spent $188.00 in the last 28 days over 15120 impressions and brought no lead.
Of 31 of our ad leads in the last 28 days, 29 were called and 22 were reached.

output.audience: Class A drivers who pull flatbed or want to, meet the opening's stated requirement, and run Midwest lanes. Many are likely in larger fleets, sharing trucks and out for longer stretches. A plain pay per mile, weekly home time and an assigned truck would stop them.

angles.idea: Lead with the pay per mile, stated plainly, over a loaded flatbed moving on a Midwest highway.
angles.proof: The opening states its pay per mile, and the work is flatbed on Midwest lanes.
angles.why: This concept brought every lead the earlier ads produced, at a cost per lead well under the benchmark's pause point, and most of those leads were reached by phone. Build on it.

angles.idea: Lead with the assigned truck, shown as a flatbed rig parked and ready for its driver.
angles.proof: The opening lists an assigned truck and flatbed work.
angles.why: Nothing has been measured for this concept. The assigned truck is a concrete fact the pay ad does not use, and showing flatbed up front tells drivers what the work is.

angles.idea: Say plainly, from the driver's seat, what this is: a small fleet where dispatch knows your name, and what it takes to apply.
angles.proof: The carrier describes itself as a small fleet where dispatch knows your name, and the opening states its requirement.
angles.why: Untested here. The lead outcomes show who picked up, not who fit, so an ad that states the licence class and the requirement lets drivers screen themselves before a recruiter calls.

angles.idea: Lead with the terms themselves as a short list on a plain plate: pay per mile, home weekly, retirement plan, assigned truck.
angles.proof: Each line on the plate is a stated fact of the opening: the pay per mile, home weekly, the retirement plan and the assigned truck.
angles.why: Not measured yet. Pay as the lead already works for this carrier, and this tests whether the full set of terms, including the retirement plan, does as well without a truck in the picture.

angles.idea: Lead with being home weekly, named alongside the Midwest lanes, over a quiet street with a driveway waiting.
angles.proof: The opening offers home weekly and runs Midwest lanes.
angles.why: The earlier version of this concept spent past the benchmark's pause point and brought no lead. Home weekly is still a real fact of the job, so try it with the lanes named, and cut it if it stalls again.
